extracted.intended_audience: theatre practitioners, dramatists, stage designers, actors, and dramatic critics
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and aesthetic criteria for mounting plays—particularly costume, colour, staging, and unity of production—grounded in historical accuracy (archæology) and illusionist method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical accuracy of costume (archæology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mount plays in the accurate costume of the time, according to the best authorities; archæology should be employed to achieve illusionist stage effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare frequently used accurate period apparel and armour as part of his illusionist method (e.g., helmets, tabards, crests). Archaeological detail provides picturesque and dramatic value. Examples: use of fifteenth-century crests in Henry VI; Jupiter, Juno, Iris and other mythic apparitions drawn from antiquarian sources. Anti-pattern: inventing arbitrary or anachronistic dress that undermines historicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of detail to central motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Details must never usurp the principal place; they should be subordinate always to the general motive of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert fact into effect and assign each detail its proper relative value. Accurate details are valuable only insofar as they increase the reality of the whole; pedantry is to be avoided. Quoted guidance from Hugo: domestic and historical details should be 'scrupulously studied and reproduced' but only to augment the overall reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume should express character without description
rubrics_metrics.description: Costume is a means of displaying character and producing dramatic situations and effects; apparel is expressive of social conditions, manners, and personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The design and character of a dress deliver dramatic information (e.g., Richard II's effeminacy reflected in dress). Avoid costumes that conflict with or obscure character traits. Examples: the 'woolvish gown' in Coriolanus as a central note of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of costume to actor and action
rubrics_metrics.description: A dress must be appropriate to the stature and appearance of the actor, to his supposed social condition, and to his necessary action in the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlaws should not appear in courtly splendour; costumes must be practical for movement required by the role. Example: Orlando's complaint in As You Like It was spoiled by over-gorgeous attire for supposed peasantry. Anti-pattern: applying sumptuary-law justifications where dramatic plausibility is harmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors must inhabit costumes (natural movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costumes should be worn as dresses, not merely as costumes; actors must be at home in their dress so movement and gesture are natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More dress rehearsals are needed so actors learn the gestures and movements conditioned by period dress (e.g., hoop-induced arm gestures in the eighteenth century; solemnity produced by a ruff). Examples of good practice: actors like Forbes-Robertson who move with ease in period attire. Anti-pattern: actors who appear embarrassed by lack of pockets or wear dress like a costume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of artistic control
rubrics_metrics.description: A really artistic production should bear the impress of one master—the whole mounting (costume, scenery, decoration) must be directed by one mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division of labour is acceptable but there must be no division of mind; the director/designer should have complete control over how each dress is to be worn and how sets harmonise with costumes. Theatre should be in the power of a 'cultured despot' to secure unity of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour harmony and whole-stage colour-scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be beauty of colour on the stage as a whole; the colour-scheme for each scene should be settled absolutely and textures tested in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid discordant mixes and glaring uses of hot reds or too much new-looking fabric. Shabbiness/faded colours can be artistically valuable for lower orders. Specific notes: blue is difficult by gaslight (peacock blue can work; light/dark blues often fail), and black is an underappreciated tone-giving neutral that can separate and harmonise colours. Example of good modern-dress background: dark grey and cream-white.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing costumes from different centuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not combine dress of different ages into one production; such medleys turn the stage into chaotic fancy dress and ruin dramatic and picturesque effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costume is a growth and evolution; dresses of one age do not harmonise artistically with those of another. Anti-pattern: creating a 'Fancy Dress Ball' of confused eras; Lytton-style suggestion that dresses need only be beautiful without being accurate is criticised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume accuracy as condition for highest beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest beauty of stage effect is not merely comparable with absolute accuracy of detail but really dependent on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventing an entirely new costume is nearly impossible except in burlesque or extravaganza. Accuracy supports pictorial and dramatic beauty; examples cited include Bancroft's eighteenth-century revivals and Irving's Much Ado About Nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background must remain background
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery and furniture should not overwhelm or distract from actors; the background should be subordinated to effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid smothering the hero in bric-à-brac, palm-trees, or excessive Louis Quatorze furniture. The background should be designed to support the figures and colour-scheme under a single artistic direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use archaeological sources for non-historical elements too
rubrics_metrics.description: Archæology is useful not only for historical plays but also for masques, mythic apparitions and other scenic elements (e.g., costumes for gods, Amazons, visions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: appearance of Jupiter on his eagle, Juno with her peacocks, Iris's many-coloured bow, and Posthumus's vision all regarded as archaeological. Research into classical sources (like Plutarch for Coriolanus) enriches dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth in art is independent of mere facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic value depends on 'Truth' rather than mere factual exactness; Truth invents or selects facts at pleasure, yet factual usage still reveals an artist's attitude toward the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare uses facts and follows chronicles like Holinshed with fidelity, yet his poetry depends on a higher Truth. Principle: use facts as means to effect, not as ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designer must control how each dress is worn
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only must dresses be designed and arranged by a master, but there must be complete control over how each dress is to be worn on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes oversight of underpinnings (avoid stiff starched petticoats under Greek dresses), how garments hang and fold, and ensuring costume lines support the intended silhouette and movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour and fabric aging as expressive tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Faded or slightly shabby fabrics can be more truthful for modern lower orders and enhance tone; costumes should not all look too new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern colours often improved by being a little faded; new-looking costumes can look garish under stage lighting. Use of black and suitable backgrounds can also enhance tonal relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect historical museum sources available
rubrics_metrics.description: Make use of extant armour, banners, robes, and other relics preserved in cathedrals, churches and the Tower as references for accurate mounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare had access to such objects in London and used them; producers should consult surviving artifacts (e.g., helms, tabards, banners) when possible to inform costume and props.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical affectation; prioritise the characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: The true dramatist aims first at what is characteristic rather than beauty for its own sake; not all characters should be made beautiful in dress or nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costume choices should reveal social types and character traits (e.g., affected dress of a society should be represented honestly). Example: Greek plays require different costume treatment than Sheridan plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide enough dress rehearsals to integrate costume and gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be far more dress rehearsals than commonly held so actors learn the gestures and movements appropriate to their historical garments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearsals reveal how garments condition movement (e.g., hoops, ruffs) and let actors stop performing costumes and start wearing clothes naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not permit small modern fads to spoil period effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Directorial tolerance of fashion concessions (e.g., insisting on modern toques or starch underdress) should be refused when they ruin delicacy of line and fold of period attire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mlle. Mars insisting on a contemporary toque in Hernani; actresses wearing starched petticoats under Greek dresses are 'wicked things' that should not be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume design must consider national and racial characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: When relevant, costume and characterisation should reflect race and national character as part of the truth of dramatic types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare's characters are stamped with the 'seal of their time' and of race (e.g., Hamlet's Northern imagination, Princess Katharine's Frenchness, Othello as true Moor). Use costume to signal such traits authentically.
